sections.h2: Before you sell in Cranberry Township
sections.html:
Cranberry is a fast-growing township in southwestern Butler County, about half an hour north of downtown Pittsburgh, and its housing market looks more like a family suburb than a small town. Because it is a township with no separate city government, nearly every step of a sale runs through three offices: the township for permits and tax certifications, Butler County for assessments, deeds and delinquent taxes, and the Seneca Valley School District for school taxes. Knowing who handles what saves time at closing, and it tells you whom to call first when a buyer asks a question you cannot answer.

If you own a house here and want to sell it, you can list it, sell it yourself, or take an as-is offer from a buyer. Each path has the same tax and paperwork steps.

An estimated 35,244 people lived in Cranberry on July 1, 2025, up from 28,098 in 2010. Three out of four households own their home, and the median home value is above $420,000. Buyers are usually working households with mortgages, who care about school district boundaries, move-in condition and inspection results. The mean commute is 27.1 minutes.

sections.h2: Taxes that come due at a Cranberry sale
sections.html:
The township's tax page lists a real estate transfer tax of 0.5 percent that goes to Cranberry, and that figure leaves out the state and school district shares. The Commonwealth takes 1 percent on top. Ask the Butler County Recorder of Deeds for the school district portion and the total on your deed, since the recorder collects the tax when the deed is filed.

Both buyer and seller are legally responsible for the realty transfer tax, and some transfers are exempt, such as certain transfers between family members and property passed by will or intestacy. Your sales contract decides who pays.

  • County and township property tax: bills mailed March 1
  • Seneca Valley School District tax: bills mailed August 1
  • Township rate for real estate, apart from county and school: 15.75 mills
  • Earned income tax: 1 percent, split between township and school district (this one follows the owner's income, not the sale)

Your closing agent will prorate the current-year taxes between you and the buyer, so having the tax bills handy at the start speeds things up.

An elected tax collector with an office in the Municipal Center on Rochester Road collects township, county and school taxes. The same office issues the certification required when a property or mobile home is sold or refinanced, reviewing the last three years of township, county and school tax records and breaking them down for the closing. The office works with real estate agents and closing attorneys, and appointments are available.

County and township bills offer a 2 percent discount within two months of the notice date. Payments after four months carry a 10 percent penalty. Taxes still unpaid after one year go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau, and a sheriff's sale follows if the balance remains unpaid for an additional year.

The Tax Claim Bureau holds its upset sale on the second Monday of September for properties two years delinquent. If a sale does not happen at that stage, the parcel goes to a judicial sale, then to a repository list. A seller with unpaid taxes should settle them or ask the Bureau for a payoff figure early, because the amount can include added costs.

Butler County's Assessment Department builds the tax bills for the county, municipalities and school districts. Assessments are still based on 1969 dollars, which is why Butler County bills use mills against a base that does not track current market value.

The county assessment page has the forms an owner may need: a Board of Assessment appeal form, a commercial or industrial appeal form, a mobile home appeal form, a homestead and farmstead exclusion application, and a change of address form. Appeal hearing information and millage sheets are posted there too.

Call the Butler County Assessment office for the current filing date and to ask whether a recent sale changes how your property is reviewed. The Seneca Valley School District runs its own homestead application window, so ask the district.

Cranberry's Code Administration staff review and inspect building, zoning, sign and fire permits and enforce the Property Code. The township follows the Pennsylvania Uniform Construction Code with the 2018 International Codes, effective October 1, 2018. Inspections are booked through the township's online portal at any hour.

Look at the work done on the house before you list. Decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences all need residential permits, and a buyer's inspector will notice an unpermitted deck or a finished basement with no paperwork. The township's code of ordinances holds the fee schedule for permits, inspections and rentals.

  • Sidewalks belong to the abutting owner, who must clear debris and handle snow and ice removal
  • Home-based businesses have their own township page and rules
  • Mobile home removal permits come from the tax collector's office

Owners selling a tenant-occupied house should ask the Code Administration office what rental fees apply.

1. Gather the current tax bills for the county, township and school district.
  2. Ask the tax collector's office for the certification and the three-year breakdown.
  3. Settle or get a payoff figure for any unpaid taxes.
  4. Locate permits for decks, sheds, pools, porches and fences.
  5. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the full transfer tax total.
  6. Have your closing agent prorate the current-year taxes.

Doing these in order keeps the closing agent from chasing paperwork in the last week, and it gives you time to fix a permit gap while the buyer is still happy to wait.

sections.h2: Which way to sell in Cranberry
sections.html:
A listing makes sense for a house in good condition that can wait for showings and a lender's appraisal. An as-is purchase suits an owner who needs a closing date: an inherited house, a relocation, a house with deferred repairs or one with unpaid taxes. In either case, compare offers by your net proceeds after transfer tax, payoffs, prorated taxes and repair credits.

Ask any buyer who is paying cash for proof of funds, the closing date, and who covers title and recording costs. Get the offer in writing before you stop marketing the house.

faqs.q: Which county handles deeds and assessments for Cranberry Township?
faqs.a: Butler County. Its Recorder of Deeds records the deed and collects transfer tax, and its Assessment Department sets the assessment and prints the tax bills.

faqs.q: Who issues the tax certification when a Cranberry house sells?
faqs.a: The township's elected tax collector, whose office is in the Municipal Center. It reviews three years of township, county and school tax records and returns a breakdown for closing.

faqs.q: Which school district taxes a Cranberry house?
faqs.a: The Seneca Valley School District. Its tax notices are mailed August 1, with a discount through September 30 and face value through November 30, and the year ends December 31.

faqs.q: What happens if I owe back taxes on a Cranberry property?
faqs.a: Unpaid taxes go to the Butler County Tax Claim Bureau after one year. A sheriff's sale can follow, and the Bureau's upset sale covers properties two years behind. Pay or request a payoff figure before you list.

faqs.q: Does a deck or shed without a permit affect a sale in Cranberry?
faqs.a: It can. Cranberry requires residential permits for decks, sheds, pools, enclosed porches and fences, and an inspector may flag unpermitted work. Ask the township's Code Administration staff how to close it out.
